title: RAJESH KUMAR versus UNION OF INDIA

paras.text:
HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Criminal Writ Petition No. 2049 of 2026
Rajesh Kumar .........Petitioner
Versus
Union of India and others ......Respondents
Presence:-
Ms. Meenakshi Arora, learned Senior Advocate (through V.C.) assisted by
Mr. Ramji Shrivastava and Ms. Vermica Semwal, Advocate for the
petitioner.
Mr. Lalit Sharma, learned Deputy Solicitor General for the Union of
India/respondent No.1.
Mr. Piyush Garg, learned Senior Advocate assisted by Mr. Kush Goswami,
Advocate for respondent-Enforcement Directorate.
Judgment reserved on 13.10.2026
Judgment delivered on 15.10.2026
Hon'ble Pankaj Purohit, J. (Oral)
The present writ petition is filed under Article 226
of the Constitution of India by the petitioner seeking
following reliefs:-
"(I) Issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of
Certiorari calling for the entire records pertaining to the
impugned search proceedings conducted on 10.09.2026
and 25.09.2026 and the summons dated 21.09.2026
issued under Section 50 of the Prevention of Money
Laundering Act, 2002 and, quash and set aside the said
impugned search proceedings, summons and all
consequential orders/actions taken pursuant thereto.
(II) Issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of
Mandamus restraining the Respondents from harassing
the Petitioner or taking any coercive measures against
the Petitioner in any manner pursuant to the impugned
search proceedings dated 10.09.2026 and 25.09.2026
and the summons dated 21.09.2026."
2. The facts in brief are that multiple FIRs including
FIR No.289 of 2022 was registered at Police Station Raipur,
District Dehradun regarding the alleged leak of the graduate
1

level examination 2021 conducted by UKSSSC. These FIRs
were clubbed together and were treated as scheduled of
offences under Prevention of Money Laundering Act
(hereinafter referred as "PMLA"). The Directorate of
Enforcement registered ECIR/DNSZO/06/2022 under
Section 3 & 4 of the PMLA in relation to the aforesaid
scheduled offences. The respondent authorities conducted
search operations under Section 17 of the PMLA at multiple
premises including the residential premise of the petitioner.
During the said search, orders under Section 17(1A) were
passed freezing the petitioner's bank account maintained with
HDFC and AXIS Bank. The respondents also issued
summons under Section 50 of PMLA to the petitioner which
were complied with by the petitioner. The statements of the
petitioner were duly recorded and the petitioner furnished
information and documents in relation to the subject matter
of investigation. Thereafter, the Directorate of Enforcement
filed prosecution complaint case no.69 of 2024 before the
learned Special Court, Dehradun in furtherance of which
cognizance was taken by the learned Special Court.
Thereafter, the respondent again on 10.09.2026 conducted the
impugned search at the same residential premises where the
search had already been taken place and in furtherance seized
two bank lockers and also confiscated one i-phone. The
respondents thereafter issued fresh summons under Section
50 of the PMLA requiring the petitioner to furnish
information and documents. Thereafter, a further search was
conducted on 24.09.2026 and on 25.09.2026, petitioner's
PNB locker was seized. The petitioner is before this Court
against the aforementioned further searches.
2

3. Learned senior counsel for the petitioner
vehemently argues that the impugned second search
conducted after filing of the prosecution complaint amounts
to an impermissible "ever greening of investigation" whereby
an investigation which had already culminated in prosecution
is sought to be repeatedly revived through coercive searches
without disclosure of any fresh material or any defined
investigative necessity. He argues that the power to search
and seizure under PMLA cannot be converted into an
unstructured and indefinite power to subject the Petitioner to
repeated searches in respect of the same allegations,
transactions and subject matter. He emphasizes that without
any requirement to demonstrate fresh material or
circumstances, the power to conduct search and seizure
indefinitely after taking cognizance under Section 17 would
reduce the statutory safeguards under Section 17 to a nullity.
He further states that such power would permit the officers to
exercise continuing coercive power over a person already
subjected to judicial proceedings, contrary to the
constitutional guarantee of fair, just and reasonable procedure
under Article 21 of the Constitution of India.
4. The learned senior counsel submits that the
provisions under Section 193 BNSS are not followed by the
Respondent authorities as once Ld. Special court is seized of
the Prosecution Complaint and is conducting trial, any further
search must be undertaken with the permission of the Ld.
Special court and not otherwise. She argues that any search
conducted in derogation of these mandatory safeguards is
arbitrary and violative of Articles 14 and 21 of the
3

Constitution of India. She submits that the speculative
assertion that the seized documents "may contain
incriminating evidence" is insufficient to override the
constitutional rights under Articles 14 and 21 of the
Constitution of India. She further submits that Section 17 of
the PMLA does not confer an unfettered or unbridled power
upon the officers of the Respondent to conduct search
proceedings according to their whims and fancies of the
respondent authorities. The expression "reason to believe"
under Section 17 is not a mere formality but a condition
precedent to the exercise of the power of search. Such belief
must be founded on relevant material in the possession of the
authorised officer and duly recorded in writing, and its
existence and rational basis are amenable to judicial scrutiny.
5. The learned Senior Counsel for the respondent-Enforcement Directorate submits that the petitioner is the
Managing Director of M/s RMS Techno Solution Pvt. Ltd.,
Lucknow and is the accused no.10 and the aforesaid
company is accused no.11 in Prosecution Complaint No.69 of
2024. He states that the aforesaid company was entrusted
with printing the papers of the graduate level exam and the
papers leaked from its printing press. The petitioner is
accused of leaking the paper and spreading it through other
accused persons. He is an accused in police charge-sheet in
FIR Nos.289 of 2022, 351 of 2022, 1 of 2020. He also
submits that the petitioner did not appear even after receiving
summons dated 18.09.2024 under Section 50 of the PMLA.
He further argues that the prosecution complaint expressly
records that the further investigation is ongoing and seeks
4

leave to file a supplementary complaint. He further submits
that the search was conducted at the premises under
authorization no.12 of 2026 dated 09.09.2026 issued under
Section 17 of the PMLA in the presence of two independent
panch witness, the authorization was shown to and signed by
the petitioner, personal search of officers was also offered
before and after the search which was denied by the
petitioner. He further states that summons dated 21.09.2026
were necessary to be issued as money laundering is a
continuing offence and the summon seeks bank's statement
up to date along with ITR updates and source of funds. He
further argues that further investigation after filing of
complaint is expressly permitted by explanation (ii) Section
44(1) of the PMLA. He further states that the aforesaid
provision was upheld in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v.
Union of India, (2022) 10 SCC 386. He also states that
explanation (ii) Section 44(1) of the PMLA specifically
provides that accused can be called for interrogation for the
purpose of recording their statements under Section 50 of the
PMLA even after filing of complaint. He further states that
the permission is required from the Court for further
investigation during the trial and not before the trial
commences. He submits that each search was conducted
after following the due process of law and after fresh
authorization under Section 17 by an officer of the rank of
Deputy Director with reasons recorded in writing and the
recorded reasons and material were forwarded to the
adjudicating authority in a sealed cover which acted as a
safeguard. He further stated that the search were necessary
as the proceeds of crime are not fully traced and against 65
5

lakhs alleged to have been received in lieu of paper leak only
11 lakhs have been recovered. He further states that as per
Section 50 the summons are a part of judicial proceeding and
the petitioner was duty bound to cooperate.
6. I have heard the rival contentions made by the
learned counsels for the parties and have perused the material
available on record.
7. Primary contention of the learned counsel for the
petitioner is that the search conducted after filing of
prosecution complaint will lead to evergreening of
investigation and is violative of Article 14 and 21 of the
Constitution of India. This Court is of the firm opinion that
the power of further investigation is enshrined in the statute
itself and Section 44 explanation (ii) of the PMLA authorizes
the same. My aforesaid view is fortified by the following
judgments of Hon'ble Apex Court. In the Assistant Director
Directorate of Enforcement v. Gautam Kundu & Anr.
Criminal Appeal arising out of SlP (Crl.) No.271 of 2024 -
Supreme Court and Bhupesh Kumar Baghel v. Union of
India & Ors. W.P. (Crl.) No.301 of 2025 - Supreme Court,
the Apex Court in these cases held that further investigation
is well open to Investigating Agency and Authorities of
Enforcement Directorate can bring on record further evidence
during trial.
8. The Court agrees with the submission of the
learned counsel for the petitioner that power to search under
Section 17 of the PMLA is not unbrittled and there are
reasonable safeguards to it. But in the case in hand fair just
and reasonable procedure has been followed by the
6

Investigating Agency and each impugned search was
authorized under Section 17 by an officer of the rank of
Deputy Director and the recorded reasons were forwarded to
the adjudicating authority in a sealed cover thereby following
the mandatory safeguard as was noted by Apex Court
Judgment in Vijay Madanlal (supra).
9. The contention of the learned counsel for the
petitioner that mandatory permission of the Court for further
investigation as enshrined under Section 193 of the BNSS,
2023 was not taken also does not hold any water as Section
193(9) of BNSS mandates prior permission of the Court only
if the further investigation is undertaken "during trial". It is a
settled proposition of law that a trial is deemed to commence
only after framing of charges and in the present case in hand
as the charges have not yet been framed, therefore,
permission of the court is not necessary. Even the
cognizance order was set aside by this Court vide order dated
25.09.2026 passed in Criminal Miscellaneous Application
No.2050 of 2026 on a limited ground of non-grant of pre-cognizance of hearing, with a direction to trial court to
proceed from the stage of cognizance.
10. Considering the above, this Court does not find
any reason to interfere with the further investigation initiated
by the Enforcement Directorate. Accordingly, the writ
petition deserves to be dismissed.
11. The writ petition is hereby dismissed.
(Pankaj Purohit, J.)
Ravi
7
